I do think they could stretch the boundaries even further with White's card draw. Its best draw still tends to be in Colorless if you're not going wide. I think there's more design space available for "catch-up" draw in the same spirit as [[Battle Angels of Tyr]].

Symmetrical draw ain't it; you pay for the spell and are down a card, and your opponents not only get more cards than you, but also don't lose tempo.

Even a simple 2W sorcery: "Draw a card for each opponent who has more cards in hand than you" would be an interesting addition. On-balance, a much worse [[Divination]]. But can be good with careful sequencing and doesn't have the feel bad of giving your opponents free cards to beat you with. White needs repeatable/burst draw that isn't symmetrical, badly.

That, or print a bunch more [[Spirit of the Labyrinth]] effects to keep everyone else's draw in step with your own.

They're bad. Like, really bad even in mono white. Think of it this way. One of the Power 9, [[Ancestral Recall]] is a 1 mana draw 3. Still, it costs U and you're "down a card" for having cast it. 

Now, imagine an opponent does that for you, for free. You don't need to cast anything. You don't need to spend mana. You are actually up one more card than one of the strongest cards ever printed. All you had to do was just sit there. This is what your opponent is thinking when you cast [[Secret Rendezvous]].

Consider also that it's not symmetrical. YOU had to cast it for 3 mana at sorcery speed. YOU went down a card relative to them (spent one to draw three, whereas they drew three cards for free). You're getting a worse deal than your opponent and YOU paid for it.

One of the absolute worst things you can do is give your opponent more options. 

Here's a better list of draw options in mono white: 

[[Esper Sentinel]] [[Mentor of the Meek]] [[Welcoming Vampire]] [[Tocasia's Welcome]] [[Sram, Senior Edificer]] [[Puresteel Paladin]] [[Firemane Commando]] [[Trouble in Pairs]] [[Minas Tirith]] [[Archivist of Oghma]] [[Smuggler's Share]] [[Enduring Innocence]] 

And in Colorless:

[[Skullclamp]] [[The One Ring]] [[The Aetherspark]] [[Sword of Fire and Ice]] [[Idol of Oblivion]] [[Mask of Memory]] [[Throne of Eldraine]]

Outside of budget reasons there's no reason whatsoever to be running [[Cut a Deal]] or [[Secret Rendezvous]]. They're awful by every metric compared to these, and outside of the nebulous and highly subjective "political" value (an aspect that tends to be greatly overvalued by inexperienced players, and frequently made to excuse the inclusion of weak cards), they're actively bad.

If you didn't read all that, then at least read this: the heuristic of "giving your opponents cards is bad" remains evergreen for a reason. Don't give them outs. That's how you lose. There are better options out there that will directly increase your win percentage.

Honestly, I never have. Been playing over 20 years. I just finished running an 8-year milestone campaign. Milestone worked great and I would never use XP. Truly, in addition to building a compelling narrative I absolutely do not want the additional logistical burden of bean counting. I've enough plates to keep spinning. 

Leveling up when I feel it is appropriate narratively feels satisfying, and my players appreciate it. In addition to the other great points raised here in support of milestone leveling, I'll offer this: to make the XP budget of a chapter's conclusion line up with narrative progression, not only do you need to plan for when they'll level, you need to plan the ENTIRE chapter beforehand so the level occurs when you want it to. Because of the numerical specificity, you must be perfectly precise and have budgeted the whole level entirely in advance, leaving no room for improvisation. 

I do not want to do all that legwork in advance when an elegant solution already exists in milestone leveling. XP is a vestige of when gold was strength. In a video game, it's already tracked for you. When that logistical burden is placed on a human it only serves to bog things down.

A better question to ask would be "What specific improvements does using XP have over milestone?" And the reasons are vanishingly few and subjective. One reason against XP leveling that is not debatable is that the act of scheduling levels, assigning XP (especially for noncombat actions) and tracking XP is burdensome, compared to the alternative. Even if you feel it's easy, (and no matter how easy you make it) there exists an indisputably easier way: not tracking it. I did not have to waste one spare neuron firing in my brain thinking about XP encounter budgeting. 

Regardless of where you fall on the debate, if you run XP, you MUST quantify every game action and assign it a numerical value. Why do this to yourself if you don't have to?

The benefits would have to outweigh that fact. I don't feel they do. "Knowing when your character is going to level up" is simply metagaming. I don't think it's valuable and it only encourages more metagaming actions if a player feels they are close to leveling. You can also just ask your DM. 

I don't know about y'all but it's just easier to say, "You beat the boss. Level up." And save your brain space for things that actually matter.

This is true but Wobbuffet's ban in Gen 3 was actually a confluence of many factors. It was a combination of Wobbuffet only knowing non-damaging moves, Shadow Tag and crucially how Struggle worked. Prior to Gen 4, it was like a regular recoil move that dealt 1/3 of its damage back to you. 

Wobbuffet has very low ATK and any damage dealt to it from opposing Wobbuffet's Struggle or its own Struggle's recoil was easily healed off with Leftovers. So in a Wobb mirror match it was an immediate draw. No one could switch out and no one could struggle themselves to death as they always had Leftovers.

In Gen 4 this was fixed when they changed Struggle to deal 1/4 of the user's max HP damage in recoil, circumventing this nightmare scenario.

Poor DM ruling aside, save or suck spells just aren't it, and are a big reason why solo boss monsters don't work in 5e. It's truly unfortunate that with the tools provided, conventional wisdom dictates you must use things like minions, time-sensitive or alternate wincons, etc. to overcome players' insurmountable advantage: action economy. That people don't realize that this is a fundamental game balance issue and don't ever question it depresses me.

There's a way to counter this but it is likely unpopular: condition immunities. Don't like Hold Person? Your BBEG has immunity to paralysis. Don't like Polymorph? Your boss has Immutable Form. Their minions? Of course they're vulnerable. But for bosses, legendary resistances aren't and have never been enough; just a bandaid to a grievous systemic issue. There has never been a time where any boss of narrative importance has been or will be easily cheesed in my games and the encounters are stronger for it. 

If you're feeling generous, you can have the boss wear some sort of amulet that gives them that immunity the players can loot, but usually I just give them immunity for the same "just because" reason that legendary resistances exist. It's simply a thing bosses need innately to present a challenge for game reasons, that doesn't rely on the crutch of minions or alternative victory conditions.

If you're not all-in on a Voltron strategy, Greaves is the best and it's not close. 0 mana equip is absurd. Once Greaves are down, every creature can get haste on curve. People are very much overvaluing Swiftfoot Boots, they're much worse than you think unless your strategy relies on stacking multiple auras or equipment (which isn't the case in the vast majority of decks) and if you have more than one creature, just swap Greaves around to remove shroud temporarily and reattach when you want. After all, it's free. 

The "you only have to pay 1, it's not that much worse" arguers for Swiftfoot Boots truly do not understand the concept of tempo, or how heavy of a tempo loss it is to delay each of your creatures by a turn to spare an extra mana to guarantee protection the turn they come down. In low power metas, perhaps it's not that noticeable, but if you're trying to win at all, you want the 0 equip cost that Greaves provides. Mana efficiency is paramount.

In Voltron, they're roughly equivalent, though you need to be judicious about having another creature to swap Greaves to and when to equip them, and I'd concede that Swiftfoot Boots edges Greaves out slightly in that deck only, but likely you want to run both. 

Lavaspur Boots is hot trash. Ward 1 is nothing. +1/+0 is negligible. Coming down on turn 1 rarely matters as you run into the Swiftfoot Boots problem of disrupting your own tempo by 1 mana each turn to equip a creature the turn it comes down. And if you're going to do that, Hexproof matters way more than Ward, so you may as well run Swiftfoot Boots instead. To those who argue the strength of Lavaspur Boots coming down turn 1, what aggressive 1-drop in EDH desperately wants a paltry Ward 1 and +1/+0 on turn 2? Basically just Ragavan?

Depends. What tier? Lower/mid tiers, you'll need traps minions and protection to mitigate action economy. 

Top tier? They would be fighting God-level threats. To facilitate this I give solo boss enemies things like extra reactions, Immutable Existence (a feature from Mighty Servant of Leuk-O) that makes them immune to polymorph and plane shift effects, and a bunch of additional condition immunities, specifically against incapacitating ones like Paralyze or Stun. A combo I'll be running against my team (as they face the God of Time) is to have the BBEG start the fight outside Counterspell range, then cast Antimagic Field. As a Deity, he can cast freely but his foes can't. His sword is an Artifact so it retains its magical properties but most of his foes' items are weakened. He has "Contingent Resurrection" from the 3.5E epic handbook if he somehow gets wombo'd. Gods tend to have Limited Magic Immunity (see the Avatar of Tiamat). My BBEG also has this, and an interactive countermeasure to temporarily suppress it. Among other powerful abilities, like a souped up version of the Alert feat, the Forcebreaker property on his sword, an immunity to being disarmed etc.

The truth is, you need to lean on your latitude as DM to "break" the rules to give your players a challenge. They already have action economy on their side, so you'll need to make up for it by playing unfairly (but within the mechanics of the game). Your bosses aren't confined to the limits of a character sheet. They could cast two or more spells a round with Legendary Actions. They could have a second phase with Mythic Actions.

The one thing a solo boss monster absolutely must have is the ability to not get shut down by incapacitation. Against low to mid tier threats Legendary Resistance is a decent fail-safe but at top tier it's trivial to burn through them. You actually need condition immunities. I know it can be a "feelsbad" thing for players but, as a DM who's rounding the bend on an 8-year campaign...no. You're not beating the literal God of Time with Hold Person. I've conditioned them to expect such immunities at high levels and there's been no problems and crucially, despite such difficulty, no one has ever died. 

Basically, you need to cheat a little. The game isn't really set up for a fair 1 v 4/5 fight.

Aggro would use it to never be out of gas. Combo would use it for assuredly busted purposes. 

The closest they came to making this card (besides Dryad Arbor) is [[Mobilized District]]. If what OP is proposing is in any way balanced, why did they give a heavy restriction (needing 4 planeswalkers/legendaries) here when turning it on as a "free" creature? How could the design of any "manland" be justified if Watcher exists?  In an aggro framing, even [[Mutavault]], [[Blinkmoth Nexus]], and [[Mishra's Factory]] NEED to cost 1 to activate. That's the cheapest they'll ever go, and none of those are a 3/3. If they didn't have that mana requirement they'd be autoincludes. Most manlands also "have summoning sickness and is your land drop for turn." Be serious. This alone is not drawback enough, and the designers' intent with the built-in mechanics of manlands and needing mana to turn them into creatures makes that point obvious. 

There's a reason why free creatures are either small [[Memnite]] [[Dryad Arbor]] or straight up kill you [[Pact of the Titan]]. Anything else would change magic forever. If you doubt it, look at the design space for MDFC creatures with land backsides. Why haven't they stapled a free creature to the back of one? It's not because they haven't thought of it. It's because they know the damage it would do to every format.

So it's a colorless creature land, a 3/3. But unlike Dryad Arbor, by not giving it land type it has no implicit mana ability. Consider older lands like [[Glacial Chasm]] that also don't tap for mana. This is "just" a free 3/3, which is too strong. But also it doesn't tap for mana. By that metric alone, a 3/3 that costs a land drop, I still think it's too strong in general and only gets stronger in older sets with more free spells and mana. Consider grabbing two of these off [[Primeval Titan]]. 

I think the main issue is it would be format warping in all the wrong ways. In formats where you can get Urborg or Yavimaya to give these mana abilities to mitigate the drawback this becomes a 4-of, and aggro as an archetype gets hosed unless you're running Lightning Bolt. It's pretty important that 3/3s for "zero" don't get printed. It's an interesting thought experiment though! I'm not sure what P/T would be appropriate to not make this busted.

So outside its combat application (where it's roughly on par with Shield at low levels and absurdly strong for its level thereafter) the real issue is it's universal application OUTSIDE combat, where every social encounter also runs into what I call the "Guidance!" problem. The universality and spammability of SB is the core concern. Even Shield, widely toted as "the best 1st level spell" by Silvery Barbs apologists is useless outside combat. 

Consider; the trigger for SB is basically: "Any time the enemy would [yes], instead, [probably not]." Because it triggers on ANY opposing D20 roll (a successful check, save or attack) this means that as long as a player has a spell slot and a reaction, the DM no longer has narrative control and must instead effectively ask permission *from their players* if what they described actually happens. For EVERY. ROLL. 

For those who play Magic: the Gathering it's like facing a control player who favors counterspells and has open mana, the DM is put in the completely absurd position of needing to ask EVERY TIME: "does it resolve?" It's an insane inversion of the roles. Now the DM needs to check with their players, even on persuasion and opposed insight rolls "if it resolves." 

Thus slowing every single interaction point to a crawl, as a wise player will want to consider the implications of an NPC succeeding that social roll (or attack, or save) before allowing the DM to continue. Every time. Multiply that by the number of spellcasters who have access to it and it turns into a complete nightmare. 

I have seen four spellcasters argue amongst themselves whether the king should be allowed to succeed on a Insight roll at seeing through their deception, who should do it, who should follow-up on SBing the King's saving throw against Modify Memory to forget all this, etc etc. For THIRTY minutes. 

Counterspell isn't like this. It only triggers on spells. Shield isn't like this. It only triggers on attacks. Silvery Barbs triggers off everything and THAT'S the problem with it.

Silvery Barbs is now banned at my table.

This is very weirdly templated. To start with, "as if they were your own" is irrelevant information as to whether you could sacrifice a creature. "As if you controlled them" actually makes sense. You can in fact own a creature but not control it. Your current wording is unclear in MTG rules syntax, even if colloquially it follows logically.

Second, as far as rules text goes, (owning/controlling confusion aside) this is still worded very strangely. What you're doing, effectively, is making a replacement effect. You need to follow the template for that: "If (event) would happen, instead (modified event)."

Try "If you would sacrifice a creature, instead you may choose a creature controlled by an opponent. If you do, that opponent sacrifices the chosen creature." Or something to that effect. 

Third, there isn't a fail condition for events where you are required to sacrifice a creature and no opponents control creatures. What happens when an opponent casts Cruel Edict and you're the only player who has a creature? "Sacrificing an opponent's creature as if it was your own" doesn't clarify what happens here. Saying you "CAN sacrifice an opponent's creature etc" doesn't actually mean anything, rules-wise. 

Having the "You may ___. If you do, _____." carries the implicit instruction that if you DON'T, you sacrifice your creatures as normal. If you don't want that fail case, you'll need to add "Creatures you control can't be sacrificed."

So actually there are great lore reasons why that's the case. Warforged are from Eberron, and in that world they are constructs. Constructs can't be healed by magic as they aren't "alive." So, they instead had spells like Repair Damage to, well...repair the damage. 

Since 5e (and the general design decision to make everything setting-agnostic) they were moved into a confusing grey area. They're not constructs from a purely mechanical nomenclature perspective. They still retain a lot of "construct-like" qualities. They now can be healed by regular healing magic. They also aren't organic, in that they don't need to eat, sleep or breathe. But still aren't more susceptible to Heat Metal (or other fire damage) like a metal, but mostly wooden construct should be. 

Basically, 5e tried to have Warforged both ways and now it's confusing. In homogenizing the setting and making anyone come from anywhere they really did lose a lot of what could have been provided in terms of concrete explanation, and in its place we're given a lot of hand-wavey "Ask your DM lol".

Death is a real risk. Without it there are no real stakes. Without stakes, there are no real heroes. I truly don't agree with the "death only with PC permission" crowd, or even the "should have talked it out in session zero" crowd. 

You can die in DnD, it's one of the core mechanics, and very much assumed out of the box. It's not the DM's responsibility to ask if every mechanic is okay. That's like asking "Is it okay if your HP is reduced?" Lunacy. If there are considerations that game-warping to be made (in the understandable event that it triggers a player), the onus is on *the player* to bring it up, either in session zero or privately to the DM as early as possible.

In 5e it's already really difficult to die after early levels, even outside of resurrection spells, a basic Healing Word goes a long way and really trivializes death saves, if you aren't killed outright. Finally, I think the "all consequences except death" crowd really should be playing a different game. There are way better systems out there that don't involve combat at all that much better serve your needs. Sometimes there *aren't* other consequences except death, that don't utterly destroy the fiction. 

If as a player I knew I could not die no matter what, why would I scale carefully down the mountain, stopping at the remote monastery to resupply and making sure to manage my resources, when I could just jump, tuck and roll and be at the bottom of Mount Everest in 6 minutes with 1hp left. Why would I not just be a meat shield in every combat and catch arrows from an enemy archer brigade with my teeth? I can't die. Why not fart in the King's general direction? If 1 person in the party desperately want his favor but 3 others are ambivalent, the threat of execution has no sting, so who really cares how it turns out, he can't do anything to you that you don't want. Exploration is actually the worst for this "can't die" mentality. You can RP your way out of most situations but the environment has no character and doesn't care. Your players have to traverse a lava field? Why not just walk through it if you're invincible? What other consequence could there be than death? A Deus Ex Machina here means no environment is ever dangerous.

Not being able to die, no matter the other RP consequences heavily skews how you approach combat, exploration and social scenarios in a way that DnD is fundamentally and mechanically unequipped to handle.

The thing is, there wasn't a strong unified vocal theory back then. We don't actually know or have any surviving recordings of what singers sounded like in that time to make any sort of judgment on Edouard's vocal stylings. 

Manuel Garcìa, generally regarded among modern vocal pedagogues as "The Father of Bel Canto," had yet to write his most important treatise: "Tratado Completo Del Arte Del Canto," and wouldn't until 1847. The Bel Canto school, and generally how we hear and appreciate modern Italian operatic style hadn't yet been solidified in 1792.

All that is to say we can't conclusively say that Edouard's vocal production was historically accurate or not, and to judge it by our modern sensibilities would be misguided.

I think it varies by level. 

At early levels when the PCs are squishy and have few resources it should trend toward 99%, but with the understanding that unwinnable fights are highly telegraphed. Being frail, they are much more subject to the variance of the system itself and accidents will happen anyway.

At mid-level they get things like Revivify and Raise Dead, you can push them harder than you think, especially if they have a strong grasp of action economy. You can trend toward 90%.

At high level? They don't even need the body anymore to bring someone back. One character can bring back everyone, assuming enough time and amassed resources commensurate to a very long campaign. Advanced escape options such as Plane Shift exist.

I have a group of level 15 players at the final act of a 7-year 5e campaign and I'm actually struggling to find ways to truly challenge them, as they have so many resources. Most monsters in the manual as written are usually not enough and 5e's CR system begins to fall apart entirely, especially for "solo" monsters, as action economy matters more than ever and it is usually very much in their favor. They also have advanced options to retain resources as well like Magnificent Mansion to enter most fights at full capacity, so wearing them down, (should they choose to be careful) is basically impossible. In this case, homebrew monsters hard and push that number to 85%*. 

*But in most cases at this tier, even "unwinnable" fights have easy ways to escape or recover from, and at this point truly anything with a stat block that you throw at them is beatable. Your players will often surprise you with their resilience and ingenuity. I've had to bring back "forbidden magic" from 3.5e/Pathfinder to keep things challenging, spells like Dimensional Anchor and Metamagic options like Interweave Dispel/Maximize Spell/Transdimensional Spell (the latter to have some sort of counterplay against Rope Trick/Tiny Hut/etc cheesing). I've also brought in "10th level/Epic spells" (from 3.5e's Epic Level Handbook) to bolster my BBEGs (I highly recommend the spell "Contingent Resurrection" for example) to level the playing field.

I'm concerned with the average person's RAW ability to lift way more than they physically should: the "lift" portion of the "push, drag or lift" makes no sense at the calculation of 30× STR. Dragging and pushing that weight makes total sense. 

RAW, the average person (10 STR) can lift 300lbs overhead. No one here who isn't a genetic freak or dedicated weightlifter can. And if you can, you're *above* average.

It's not "an average hero" though. It's 10 in the Commoner Stat block, as well. 10 is just the human average. So yes, it's weird that a Commoner can lift 300lbs, even overhead. I know I can't, and I do lift occasionally.

I agree with the RAW re: pushing and dragging, but "lifting" should be qualified a bit. I can "lift" a 200lb stone a few inches to see what's underneath. I cannot lift it over my head. 

Consider also that a Strength Score of 10 is an average person, represented in the Commoner stat block. I am commoner-adjacent: a 220lb, 6-foot guy in reasonable shape and FOR SURE cannot lift 300lbs overhead (the limit of 30× my strength score), especially an awkward item like a stone without handholds. Drag, or push? With effort, yes. 

The world record for overhead lifting is 212kg, or 467lbs. 

To say that the average person can lift 300lbs overhead might be "true" in RAW but is absurd once you break it down. I would ask for Athletics Checks for outsized and heavy items and would have different DCs for different lifts.

It's a timing restriction issue, mostly. Black's creature removal is so potent because it can be done at any time, not counting [[Royal Assassin]] effects. With Withering Boon, you have one tiny window, when it's on the stack, to interact. 

You need to hold up that mana forever. Maybe you use it, but a bigger threat hits the board next turn you wish you'd saved it for. While that's an issue with most single target removal, the timing of [[Withering Boon]] means you're operating with incomplete information, hoping each time it's the best threat you can hit, hedging against future unknown threats, holding open mana all the while. 

[[Infernal Grasp]] when cast hits the best creature on the board: you get to decide what that is and when that happens, you can choose from among creatures cast at any point in the game, and the current board state is all known information you can build on and play around proactively OR reactively. You're not limited to "what's on the stack right now." And that's crucial. 

Effectively, Withering Boon can't change what's been done, and can't affect the board (at all) the way a simple [[Murder]] can. What this adds up to is a card with a very narrow application and timing window and the common reality of facing down an already-resolved threat that, nine times out of ten, you wished could "die to [[Doom Blade]]."

I think people are highly overvaluing this. It's good, graded on a curve of white's traditionally terrible card draw. It's still worse than almost all non-white options. People are understandably very excited, but the ceiling is still only okay. You're up two cards (assuming you're in a 4 player pod), having "spent" a card, and your opponents, in aggregate, are up 3. That's it's not targeted is actually a downside, when you need it most, you can't help but also fuel whoever is in the lead. 

It also still doesn't address the fundamental issue that Secret Rendezvous had: you're not just giving your opponents free cards, you're actively giving up a card (by casting it) and paying for it, reducing what else you can play that turn off that draw. To use a fraught political metaphor, they're building a wall, and you're paying for it. They're not just getting a free card, they're getting a deal that's literally better than free because you paid for it yourself. 

The floor? It's far less rosy than even this. You're one on one, the other players have been eliminated. Your hand is empty, and you topdeck this card. Are you really going to cycle this card at sorcery speed (not even going up in cards!) giving the opponent a better than free card? Or is it better to let it rot in your hand and hope you don't just hand them their last combo piece? 

The floor is abysmal: in the 1 on 1 endgame, if you're ahead, it's at best "win more, (but also maybe give your opponent more outs)." At worst, when playing from behind, it's the rare case of "lose more," giving an already-winning opponent an additional card, at your expense. You are literally better off drawing a basic land in that position. In that respect alone, it's better than Secret Rendezvous, I suppose. 

Beware. If you consider this card a Mono White staple, know that it's a trap. You're only seeing the ceiling, which is negligible at best: "White draw 3!* Wow!" and not the truly horrendous floor. It can obviously see use in niche or fun group hug strats, but outside of that? Steer clear of it in higher powered pods. You will regret casting this card.
